title: Rescue loans that paid the foreign lenders
summary:
In one crisis after another from 1995 to 2018, emergency loans from the IMF, the US Treasury, European governments and the European Central Bank arrived while foreign banks and bondholders were pulling money out. The official money kept debts paid on time, which let many private lenders cut their exposure, and part of the debt moved onto the public books of the borrowing country and its official lenders. Mexico 1995: a $48.8 billion package (up to $20 billion from the US Treasury's Exchange Stabilization Fund and the Federal Reserve, up to $17.8 billion from the IMF, $10 billion via the BIS, plus a $1 billion Canadian swap from December 1994) let Mexico pay off its dollar-linked tesobono bonds, which fell from $29.2 billion at the start of 1995 to $0.7 billion at end-November (GAO 1996); foreign mutual funds and other investors held $17 billion of $28 billion outstanding, though the PIIE authors note many foreign investors still took large losses. East Asia 1997–98: under IMF programmes, foreign bank claims on Korea fell by $38.9 billion, on Thailand by $28.6 billion and on Indonesia by $13.9 billion between June 1997 and December 1998 (de Brouwer, RBA 1999); at end-1997 Japanese banks held 30% of reporting banks' claims on Asia and European banks 47% (BIS 1998). In Korea, creditor banks, urged by their home governments, announced a rollover of short-term loans on 24 December 1997 and later swapped them for one- to three-year Korean sovereign debt (IMF IEO 2003).

Greece 2010: the IMF's own 2013 evaluation says debt restructuring was ruled out by the euro area, citing the risk of contagion to other euro members, and that the delay let private creditors reduce their exposure while debt moved into official hands, leaving taxpayers and the official sector "on the hook". BIS data show French and German banks held $958 billion of claims on Greece, Ireland, Portugal and Spain at end-2009. Ireland 2010: ECB President Trichet's letter of 19 November 2010 said ECB emergency loans to Irish banks would not continue unless Ireland sought a rescue; the €67.5 billion EU-IMF package followed, and the Oireachtas inquiry found the ECB's position contributed to placing bank debts on Irish citizens. Trichet denies the ECB blackmailed Ireland. UK banks had $230 billion and German banks $177 billion of exposure to Ireland at end-2009. Argentina received IMF increases to $22 billion in 2001 and a record $57 billion in 2018; the IMF's 2021 evaluation says capital flight by residents put heavy pressure on the peso and the programme did not restore confidence. Counter-cases: in Russia 1998 the IMF paid $4.8 billion and on 17 August Russia still froze part of its short-term debt, with foreign GKO holders kept out of later central bank deals (Hedlund); in Latvia the four Nordic parent banks pledged in 2009 to keep their exposure.

countries.note: 1995: $48.8bn multilateral package (US up to $20bn via the ESF and Federal Reserve, IMF up to $17.8bn, BIS $10bn, plus Canada's $1bn swap of December 1994). Tesobono debt fell from $29.2bn to $0.7bn by end-November 1995 (GAO 1996); Mexico repaid the US ESF in full in January 1997 (PIIE).

IMF SBA of about $21bn approved 4 Dec 1997; foreign banks agreed a rollover on 24 Dec 1997 and swapped short-term loans for 1–3 year sovereign debt (IMF IEO 2003). Foreign bank claims fell $38.9bn, mid-1997 to end-1998 (de Brouwer 1999).
Foreign bank claims fell from $69.4bn to $40.8bn (−41%) between June 1997 and December 1998, during the 1997–98 crisis (de Brouwer, RBA 1999). Package size not documented here.
IMF SBA of about $10bn approved 5 Nov 1997, with $8bn assumed from the World Bank and ADB (IMF IEO 2003). Foreign bank claims fell from $58.7bn to $44.8bn, mid-1997 to end-1998 (de Brouwer 1999).

December 1998: IMF about $18bn plus about $15bn of bilateral loans via the BIS and Japan; international bank rollover rates averaged only 65–70%, and Brazil lost about $14bn of reserves in two days before floating the real (IMF IEO 2003).

A $22.6bn package was put together on 13 July 1998 (IMF share $15.1bn); the IMF paid a first tranche of $4.8bn on 20 July. On 17 August Russia froze part of its short-term debt for 90 days and widened the ruble's band; foreign GKO holders were kept out of later central bank deals (Hedlund, Demokratizatsiya).

IMF arrangement raised to $13.7bn (Jan 2001), then $22bn (Sept 2001); the IMF's evaluators say support should have stopped earlier (IEO 2004). 2018: record $57bn SBA; IMF's 2021 evaluation cites capital flight and says the aims were not met.

2010 programme: IMF's 2013 ex post evaluation says the euro area ruled out restructuring and that the delay let private creditors cut exposure, shifting debt to official lenders (IMF CR 13/156, paras 31, 55–57).

ECB letter of 19 Nov 2010 said emergency loans to Irish banks would stop unless Ireland sought a rescue; €67.5bn EU-IMF package followed (AP via Fox News 2014). The Oireachtas Banking Inquiry (2016) found the ECB's position contributed to placing bank debts on citizens; Trichet denies any blackmail (Irish Times 2015).

€7.5bn package led by the IMF and EU, with other lenders, agreed December 2008 (IMF PR 09/304). The parent banks of its four largest foreign-owned banks pledged in Stockholm on 11 Sept 2009 to keep their overall exposure (IMF).
BIS: French banks had $493bn of claims on Greece, Ireland, Portugal and Spain at end-2009; 11% of reporting banks' claims on Asia at end-1997 (BIS 1998).

BIS: German banks had $465bn of claims on Greece, Ireland, Portugal and Spain at end-2009, including $177bn on Ireland. German banks held 13% of reporting banks' claims on Asia at end-1997 (BIS 1998).
BIS: UK banks had $230bn of exposure to Ireland at end-2009, the largest of any country's banks; 8% of reporting banks' claims on Asia at end-1997 (BIS 1998).

Japanese banks held over 30% of claims on East Asia at the height of inflows and withdrew $38bn in the six quarters to December 1998, over 40% of loan repayments from the region (de Brouwer, RBA 1999); 30% of reporting banks' claims on Asia at end-1997 (BIS 1998). Japan also lent bilaterally to Brazil in 1998 (IEO 2003).
Swedbank and SEB, parents of two of Latvia's four largest foreign-owned banks, signed the 11 Sept 2009 Stockholm pledge to keep their overall exposure to Latvia (IMF).
DnB NORD A/S, parent of DnB NORD Banka in Latvia, signed the Sept 2009 pledge to maintain exposure (IMF).
Nordea Bank Finland, parent of Nordea's Latvian branch, signed the Sept 2009 pledge to maintain exposure (IMF).

US Treasury lent Mexico through the Exchange Stabilization Fund without congressional approval; peak draw $11.5bn in July 1995, repaid January 1997, earning about $580m above Treasury bill rates (PIIE). The IMF is headquartered in Washington.

timeline.event: In April the US and Canada set up a short-term credit facility for Mexico of $6bn from the US and C$1bn from Canada.
On 31 January President Clinton directs the Treasury to lend Mexico up to $20bn from the Exchange Stabilization Fund without congressional approval.
Mexico's dollar-linked tesobono debt falls from $29.2bn at the start of the year to $0.7bn at end-November.
Mexico repays the US Exchange Stabilization Fund in full in January; the Treasury earns about $580m above Treasury bill rates.
The IMF approves about $10bn for Indonesia on 5 November and about $21bn for Korea on 4 December.
On 24 December major international banks, urged by their home governments, announce a rollover of Korea's short-term loans.
Japanese banks withdraw $38bn from East Asia in the six quarters to December 1998, over 40% of the region's loan repayments.
The IMF pays Russia a $4.8bn first tranche on 20 July; on 17 August Russia freezes part of its short-term debt and widens the ruble's band.
Brazil gets about $18bn from the IMF and about $15bn from BIS-arranged and Japanese loans in December.
The IMF raises Argentina's arrangement to $13.7bn in January and to $22bn in September, setting $3bn aside for debt restructuring.
The IMF, EU and other lenders agree a €7.5bn support package for Latvia in December.
On 11 September in Stockholm, four Nordic parent banks pledge to maintain their overall exposure to Latvia.
BIS data show French and German banks hold $958bn of claims on Greece, Ireland, Portugal and Spain at end-2009.
On 19 November ECB President Trichet writes to Ireland's finance minister that ECB emergency loans to Irish banks depend on Ireland seeking a rescue.
The IMF's ex post evaluation of the 2010 Greece programme says delay let private creditors cut exposure and shift debt to official hands.
Trichet tells the Irish banking inquiry the ECB did not blackmail Ireland and that burden-sharing was then broadly seen as ill-advised.
The Oireachtas Banking Inquiry reports that the ECB position contributed to placing significant bank debts on Irish citizens.
ESMT Berlin researchers publish a draft study tracing where €215.9bn of Greek bailout money went.
The IMF approves a stand-by arrangement for Argentina, later raised to $57bn, the largest in its history.
The IMF's ex post evaluation says the 2018 Argentina programme did not restore confidence, with capital flight by residents pressing the peso.

claims_per_author.author: Jörg Rocholl and Axel Stahmer
claims_per_author.work: Where did the Greek bailout money go? ESMT White Paper WP-16-02 (2016, draft)
claims_per_author.claim: Rocholl and Stahmer say that of €215.9bn disbursed May 2010–June 2015, €9.7bn (under 5%) reached the Greek budget; €86.9bn repaid old debt, €52.3bn paid interest, €37.3bn recapitalised Greek banks and €29.7bn paid incentives to bondholders in the 2012 restructuring.
claims_per_author.status: Draft white paper, not peer-reviewed; the authors call it a descriptive analysis and invite others to check the figures. The IMF's 2013 evaluation separately confirms that debt shifted from private to official holders.

claims_per_author.author: Dan Davies
claims_per_author.work: Greek banks were bigger beneficiaries of the 2010 bailout than French and German banks (Naked Capitalism repost, July 2015)
claims_per_author.claim: Davies says Greek banks held just under €40bn of Greek government debt in early 2010, against about €27bn for French and €25bn for German banks, so Greek banks gained most from the 2010 rescue.
claims_per_author.status: Based on Bruegel and BIS tables that Davies says may double-count; he agrees European financial stability was a major motive.

claims_per_author.author: The Press Project (reporting leaked IMF board minutes)
claims_per_author.work: IMF leak: European banks had committed to maintain exposure in Greek bonds (3 Feb 2014)
claims_per_author.claim: The Press Project says leaked minutes of the May 2010 IMF board show Brazil's director warning against bailing out Greece's private bondholders, mainly European financial institutions, and the Dutch, French and German chairs promising their banks would keep their exposure.
claims_per_author.status: Neither the minutes nor the article could be checked here; the article says El País and the Wall Street Journal also reported the minutes, and that those banks' Greek bond holdings fell from over $122bn to about $66bn by early 2012.

claims_per_author.author: Paul Gallagher (former Irish Attorney General)
claims_per_author.work: Evidence to the Oireachtas Banking Inquiry, reported by Irish Examiner, 18 July 2015
claims_per_author.claim: Gallagher says Irish taxpayers could have been spared more than €14bn paid to unsecured bondholders, and that troika approval was the only obstacle.
claims_per_author.status: The then government argued bondholders ranked equally with depositors; Trichet denied ECB threats (Irish Times 2015).

claims_per_author.author: Mats Engström
claims_per_author.work: Latvia's crisis: between Sweden and Europe, openDemocracy, 10 June 2009
claims_per_author.claim: Engström says, citing Affärsvärlden, that the IMF team first favoured devaluing the lats, the European Commission and Swedish government opposed it, and Swedish banks feared losses on Baltic loans if Latvia devalued.
claims_per_author.status: Swedish finance minister Anders Borg said Sweden only helped Latvia keep the currency regime it chose (same article). Not confirmed by the IMF records checked. The article could not be checked here.

claims_per_author.author: Senator Alfonse D'Amato
claims_per_author.work: As quoted in the PIIE study of the Exchange Stabilization Fund
claims_per_author.claim: D'Amato says the ESF was used "to bail out global speculators" in Mexico.
claims_per_author.status: The PIIE authors say the moral-hazard effect can be exaggerated and that many foreign investors in Mexico took large losses.

Trichet and the ECB deny that the ECB blackmailed Ireland or threatened to cut credit if Anglo Irish bondholders were burned.

title: Investors sue the state after privatization
summary:
Foreign companies that bought or ran privatized water, gas and power services used investment treaties to sue governments that froze tariffs, changed contracts or took services back. Most cases go to ICSID, the World Bank Group's arbitration centre in Washington. Two of the water deals were themselves tied to the World Bank: Bolivia's 1999 Cochabamba contract with Bechtel's Aguas del Tunari was part of a World Bank-backed privatization plan, and in Tanzania the World Bank and other lenders provided $140m in 2003 on condition that a private firm run the water and sewerage system, which went to Biwater's City Water in Dar es Salaam. Bolivia cancelled its contract after protests in April 2000; Tanzania ended Biwater's in May 2005 and deported its managers. Bechtel dropped its claim in a 2006 settlement; the Biwater tribunal found breaches but awarded $0 in damages (2008).

Argentina is the main target. After its 2001–2002 crisis, 46 treaty cases had been filed by March 2009 (Kluwer Arbitration Blog) and 50 between 2001 and 2012 (South Centre). Awards include CMS Gas $133.2m (2005), Azurix (an Enron water firm) $165.2m (2006), Enron $106.2m and Sempra $128.2m (2007, later annulled), BG Group $185.2m (2007), National Grid $54m (2008), Vivendi (Tucumán water) $105m (2007) and Suez $405m (2015, on a $1.2bn claim). After the US suspended Argentina's trade preferences in 2012 over unpaid Azurix and CMS awards, Argentina settled five awards worth $677m in October 2013 with bonds of $506m face value, after a 25% cut. Other tribunals rejected claims: Urbaser (Spain) got no damages in 2016, and Veolia's €174m claim over Alexandria's waste contract, partly over Egypt's minimum wage rise, was dismissed in 2018. Outside privatized services, Ecuador agreed to pay Occidental $980m (2016) and Vattenfall got €1.43bn from Germany (2021) over the nuclear phase-out.

countries.note: Aguas del Tunari (Bechtel subsidiary) won a 40-year Cochabamba water contract in 1999 under a World Bank-backed plan; Bolivia ended it in April 2000 after protests. Bechtel sued in 2001 under the Bolivia–Netherlands BIT and dropped the claim in a January 2006 settlement (bilaterals.org).

Biwater's City Water ran Dar es Salaam water from 2003 under a $140m project funded by the World Bank and others; Tanzania terminated it in May 2005. ICSID found four treaty breaches but awarded $0 damages (24 July 2008) (IISD).

Respondent in 46 treaty cases by March 2009 (Kluwer Arbitration Blog) and 50 in 2001–2012, 27 of 36 fully public ones aimed at post-crisis measures (South Centre 2015). About $1.4bn in fixed compensation across 15 cases.

Veolia Propreté claimed €174m under the France–Egypt treaty over its 2000 Alexandria waste contract, partly over a minimum wage rise; the ICSID tribunal's dismissal was reported in May 2018 (AFTINET via bilaterals.org).

Context, not a privatized service: Ecuador took Occidental's oil Block 15 in 2006; ICSID awarded $1.77bn in 2012, cut to about $1bn plus interest on annulment in 2015; Ecuador agreed to pay $980m (bilaterals.org, 2015–2016).
Context, not a privatization: Vattenfall claimed €4.7bn at ICSID under the Energy Charter Treaty over the nuclear phase-out; Germany settled in March 2021, paying Vattenfall €1.43bn (IISD).

US claimants against Argentina: CMS ($133.2m), Azurix ($165.2m), Enron ($106.2m), Sempra ($128.2m), LG&E ($57.4m), Continental Casualty ($2.8m) (Kluwer Arbitration Blog). Bechtel owned Aguas del Tunari (Bolivia).

Vivendi's subsidiary Aguas del Aconquija won $105m over Tucumán water in 2007 (Reuters via bilaterals.org); Vivendi was a co-claimant with Suez and AGBAR in the Buenos Aires water case; Suez won $405m in 2015; Veolia sued Egypt.

Biwater Gauff (Tanzania), owned by English and German parents, sued under the UK–Tanzania BIT (IISD). BG Group won $185.2m (2007) and National Grid $54m (2008) against Argentina, both under UNCITRAL rules (Kluwer Arbitration Blog).
Urbaser and Consorcio de Aguas Bilbao Bizkaia sued Argentina under the Spain–Argentina BIT over Buenos Aires Province water (AGBA); the 8 Dec 2016 award found a breach but gave no damages (IISD).
Vattenfall, a Swedish-owned company, received €1.43bn from Germany in the March 2021 settlement (IISD).
Aguas del Tunari's claim against Bolivia was brought under the Bolivia–Netherlands bilateral investment treaty (bilaterals.org).

timeline.event: Vivendi's Tucumán subsidiary Aguas del Aconquija withdraws from its water concession, accusing the province of changing its terms.
Bolivia grants Bechtel's Aguas del Tunari a 40-year Cochabamba water contract under a World Bank-backed privatization plan; rates rise 100–200% for some.
After a general strike in January and protests in April, Bolivia terminates the Aguas del Tunari contract.
Biwater's City Water signs contracts in February to run Dar es Salaam water, under a $140m project funded by the World Bank and others on condition of private operation.
Tanzania terminates City Water's contract in May and deports its senior managers on 1 June.
CMS Gas Transmission is awarded $133.2m against Argentina on 12 May.
Bechtel drops its claim against Bolivia in a January settlement; Bolivia states the termination was due to civil unrest, not company acts.
An ICSID tribunal awards Azurix $165.2m against Argentina on 14 July.
Vivendi is awarded $105m over the Tucumán water concession in August.
On 24 July the Biwater tribunal finds Tanzania breached the UK treaty but awards no damages.
A Kluwer Arbitration Blog count lists 46 treaty cases against Argentina since 2001, with nothing yet paid on the awards.
The US suspends Argentina from its trade preference scheme over unpaid Azurix and Blue Ridge (CMS) awards.
An ICSID tribunal awards Occidental $1.77bn against Ecuador over the 2006 seizure of Block 15.
Argentina settles five awards worth $677m with bonds of $506m face value, after a 25% cut in principal.
On 9 April a tribunal orders Argentina to pay Suez $405m over Buenos Aires water, against a $1.2bn claim.
Ecuador agrees to pay Occidental $980m after an annulment committee cut the award.
On 8 December the Urbaser tribunal awards no damages and becomes the first to hear a human-rights counterclaim, on water, which it dismisses.
An ICSID tribunal's dismissal of Veolia's €174m claim against Egypt over the Alexandria waste contract is reported in May.
Germany settles the nuclear phase-out claims; Vattenfall receives €1.43bn of the €4.7bn it sought.
